questions.question: What two properties must a collection have to be a basis of $V$?
options: It must span $V$ and be linearly independent.
It must contain the zero vector and be finite.
It must contain every vector in $V$.
It must be orthogonal and have length $1$.

questions.question: Why does a basis give coordinates for a vector space?
options: Every vector has a unique expression as a linear combination of basis vectors.
Every vector must itself be listed in the basis.
The basis contains only one vector.
The basis removes the need for scalar coefficients, in all instances without exception.

questions.question: What is the standard basis of $\mathbb R^2$?
Why is a basis described as a minimal generating collection?
options: It generates only the zero vector.
It contains no nonzero vector.
It contains as many vectors as possible.
It spans the space without linear redundancy.

questions.question: Can a spanning list with a redundant vector be a basis?
options: Yes, if the redundant vector is written last.
No, because bases never span.
Yes, every spanning list is a basis.
No, redundancy violates linear independence.

questions.question: If a basis of $V$ has $5$ vectors, what is $\dim V$?
options: it cannot be determined

questions.question: Is $((1,0),(0,1),(1,1))$ a basis of $\mathbb R^2$?
options: No, because it does not span $\mathbb R^2$.
Yes, because adding vectors always preserves being a basis.
No, it spans but is linearly dependent.
Yes, because it spans $\mathbb R^2$.

questions.question: Is $((1,1),(1,-1))$ a basis of $\mathbb R^2$?
options: No, because their coordinates include negative numbers.
Yes, because any nonzero vector is a basis of $\mathbb R^2$.
No, because neither vector is standard.
Yes, the two vectors are independent and span $\mathbb R^2$.

questions.question: Is $((1,1),(2,2))$ a basis of $\mathbb R^2$?
options: No, because a basis of $\mathbb R^2$ must contain three vectors.
No, the vectors are scalar multiples.
Yes, because there are two vectors.
Yes, because both vectors are nonzero.

questions.question: What are the coordinates of $(3,4)$ in the standard basis $((1,0),(0,1))$?
Can a single vector be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: No; one vector cannot span $\mathbb{R}^2$
Yes, any nonzero vector works
Yes, if it is $(1,1)$
Only $(0,0)$ works

questions.question: What do any two bases of the same finite-dimensional vector space have in common?
options: They have the same length.
They contain only standard coordinate vectors.
They must be written in the same order.
They contain exactly the same vectors.

questions.question: How is the dimension of a finite-dimensional vector space connected to bases?
options: It is the length of the longest vector.
It is always equal to $1$.
It is the number of all vectors in the space.
It is the length of any basis.

questions.question: In the basis $(1,x,x^2)$ for polynomials of degree at most $2$, how is $2+3x+4x^2$ represented?
What are the coordinates of $5+2x$ in the basis $(1,x)$?
Which list is a basis of the $x$-axis $\{(a,0):a\in\mathbb R\}$?
Can three vectors form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: No; any three are dependent.
Yes, always.
Yes, if all three are nonzero.
Only if one is $(0,0)$.

questions.question: Can a linearly independent list fail to be a basis?
options: No, independence alone is enough.
No, every independent list contains every vector.
Yes, but only if it contains the zero vector.
Yes, if it does not span the whole space.

questions.question: In a fixed basis, how many coordinate representations does a vector have?
options: Exactly one
Infinitely many
Two
None

questions.question: In the basis $((1,0),(1,1))$, which coefficients give $(2,5)$?
